title: Analysis: ‘Super El Niño’ reaches ‘remarkable’ all-time record - Carbon Brief
gist: The 2026 El Niño has hit a Niño 3.4 anomaly of 3.07C as of 19 September, tying the November 2015 all-time daily record two months earlier in the season than records are normally set. Fourteen seasonal forecast models project a peak of roughly 4.1C between November and January — every single one of 674 model runs exceeds the 2015-16 record — with the resulting global temperature impact landing mostly in 2027 rather than 2026.

insights.claim: As of 19 September 2026 the daily Niño 3.4 sea surface temperature anomaly stands at 3.07C, a statistical tie with the all-time record of 3.08C set on 18 November 2015.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A benchmark-equalling ocean anomaly already reached is the hard input for commodity and agricultural weather risk models.
insights.quote: As of 19 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region stands at 3.07C, putting it in a statistical tie with the previous record of 3.08C.
insights.locator: The strength of an event is tracked

insights.claim: The record-equalling anomaly is most notable for its timing, because El Niño typically peaks in the winter months of November or December, leaving two or more months of further strengthening ahead.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Calendar timing, not the current level, is what implies the event is far from its ceiling.
insights.quote: this is remarkable, in part because of how early in the calendar year it is occurring

insights.claim: Every strong El Niño on record has continued to strengthen after mid-September, providing a historical base rate that argues the current event has not peaked.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A clean historical base rate to lean on when the models and observations disagree.
insights.quote: Every strong El Niño on record has continued to strengthen after mid-September – and there is every reason to think that this one will as well.
insights.locator: El Niño typically peaks in the winter months

insights.claim: The 2026 event has been developing faster than any previous El Niño on record, having been underway since June with strength exceeding every other year from that point onward.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Speed of onset compresses the lead time available to hedge weather-sensitive exposures.
insights.quote: Since the start of June, El Niño’s strength has been greater than any other year.
insights.locator: If ONI is calculated using a baseline of 1991-2020

insights.claim: In early September of both 1997 and 2015, anomalies were around 1.9C — more than a full degree below the 2026 reading at the same calendar point.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The gap versus the two benchmark super-El Niños is unusually wide, so analogue-year playbooks likely understate impacts.
insights.quote: In early September in both 1997 and 2015, anomalies were around 1.9C – more than one degree below where they are this year.

themes.theme: Which index you use changes the story

insights.claim: Whether a new El Niño record has already been set depends on the baseline chosen: using a 1991-2020 baseline for the Oceanic Niño Index, the current event has already set a new record, while other conventions leave it tied.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Headline 'record broken' claims will diverge across outlets — check the baseline before reacting to a data print.
insights.quote: If ONI is calculated using a baseline of 1991-2020 then the current El Niño has already set a new record.
insights.locator: If ONI is calculated using a baseline

insights.claim: The Oceanic Niño Index subtracts the latest 30-year regional average from daily sea surface temperatures, which deliberately removes much of the influence of longer-term human-driven warming from the measure.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The standard index is already detrended, so El Niño records are not simply an artefact of background warming.
insights.quote: It removes much of the influence of longer-term, human-driven warming from the index.

insights.claim: NOAA's relative Oceanic Niño Index, introduced in 2024, subtracts tropical ocean anomalies between 20 degrees north and south, which can systematically understate very strong events whose warmth extends well beyond the Niño 3.4 region.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: RONI-based commentary will look more benign than reality for events of this scale; do not treat it as the neutral measure.
insights.quote: can also diminish the apparent strength of strong El Niño events, such as the current one, which extend well outside the Niño 3.4 region

insights.claim: RONI stood at around 2.5C in mid-September 2026 — record-setting for the time of year but 0.7C below the all-time daily record set in late December 1982, at the peak of that event.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The like-for-like comparison is mid-September to mid-September, not mid-September to another event's December peak.
insights.quote: RONI stood at around 2.5C in mid-September, some 0.7C below the 1982 record.
insights.locator: The chart below shows daily RONI values

insights.claim: Past events added between 0.5C and 1.9C to their RONI values between mid-September and their peak, implying the current event's 2.5C reading would likely also exceed the 1982 record if it follows historical trajectories.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Even on the conservative index the all-time record is within reach — a quantified range for scenario planning.
insights.quote: The 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16 events added between 0.5C and 1.9C to their RONI values between mid-September and their peaks.
insights.locator: However, that record was set in late December

insights.claim: August 2026 recorded a Niño 3.4 anomaly of around 2.45C, higher than the peak of every prior El Niño event on record except 2015-16 (2.75C) and 1877-78 (around 2.7C, reconstructed from sparse ship data).
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A pre-peak monthly average already ranking third in 150 years sets an unusually high floor for the eventual outcome.
insights.quote: This is higher than the peak of every prior El Niño event on record except 2015-16 – where the anomaly reached 2.75C – and 1877-78

insights.claim: Fourteen seasonal forecast models collectively project a peak monthly Niño 3.4 anomaly of around 4.1C later this year, with 80% of 674 individual model runs falling between 3.4C and 4.6C.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A tight multi-model band around 4.1C is a tradeable central case for agricultural, hydro and energy-demand exposures.
insights.quote: the models project a peak monthly anomaly later this year of around 4.1C, with 80% of the 674 individual model runs falling between 3.4C and 4.6C

insights.claim: Every single one of the 674 model runs peaks above the 2015-16 record, and the projected 1.3C margin over that record is larger than the entire gap between the strongest and fifth-strongest El Niño of the past 150 years.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Unanimous model agreement plus an unprecedented margin means the tail scenario is the central scenario here.
insights.quote: The projected margin over that record, some 1.3C, is larger than the entire gap between the strongest and fifth-strongest El Niño of the past 150 years.
insights.locator: Every single model run peaks above

insights.claim: No seasonal forecast system has ever been verified against an El Niño event of this size because none has ever occurred, and the models already ran about 0.3C warm versus observed August temperatures.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: The 4.1C central forecast is out-of-sample and shows a warm bias — size positions for a distribution, not a point estimate.
insights.quote: No seasonal forecast system has ever been verified against an event of this size, because none has ever occurred.

themes.theme: 2027 is the year that gets hit

insights.claim: El Niño's effect on global temperatures typically lags rising Pacific ocean temperatures by several months, so most of the warming impact from the 2026 event will be felt in 2027 rather than 2026.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: Position for 2027 climate-record headlines, policy pressure and weather-driven commodity disruption, not 2026's numbers.
insights.quote: so most of the impact will be felt in 2027 rather than 2026
insights.locator: El Nino’s effect on global temperatures typically lags

insights.claim: 2026 is already on track to be the warmest or second-warmest year on record according to the latest quarterly state-of-the-climate analysis — before the lagged effect of the current El Niño has even landed.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A near-record year plus a lagged record El Niño stacks two upward forces on 2027's temperature print.
insights.quote: found 2026 on track to be the warmest or second-warmest year on record
insights.locator: Carbon Brief’s most recent “state of the climate”

insights.claim: If the multi-model forecast holds, the current event will peak between November 2026 and January 2027 at a level far beyond any event previously observed in the instrumental record.
insights.speaker: Zeke Hausfather
insights.so_what: A specific two-to-three month window in which to expect maximum weather disruption and headline risk.
insights.quote: the current event will peak between November and January at a level far beyond any event previously observed in the instrumental record
insights.locator: However, all strong El Niño events on record
